title: Chitta: Memory, Saṁskāra and Pattern Continuity
reflection: Tend the field this week: let one old channel go unfed, and carve one clearer channel by repeating one small, kind practice.

questions.q: What is chitta, according to Conversation 2.6?
o: The memory-field, the riverbed: the channel that decides where today’s water goes.
The radar of the mind: the worker that scans, compares and flags what is new.
The decider of the mind: the worker that settles what a thing is and what it means.
The I-maker of the mind: the worker that stamps each experience as mine.
questions.e: Present experience is the water flowing now; chitta is the channel it flows through. Every past experience carved that channel. The carved channels are saṁskāras, stored tendencies that shape what happens next.
questions.c: Chitta is the riverbed: the field of stored tendencies

questions.q: “Chitta grooves only the painful experiences, and leaves the good ones to fade.”
questions.e: Chitta grooves the good and the painful alike. A childhood of scolding cuts a groove of shame, and years of practice cut grooves of effortless skill or calm. The question is never whether it grooves but what gets grooved.
questions.c: Chitta grooves the good and the painful alike

questions.q: A man can disprove a worrying thought and still have it return unchanged. Why, in Conversation 2.6?
o: His knowing is a ripple on the surface; the saṁskāra is carved into the bed beneath.
His arguments are weak, so that a better argument would put the thought to rest.
His memory is poor, so that he forgets the proof each time the thought returns.
His thought is true, so that it comes back because no proof could ever remove it.
questions.e: A ripple cannot re-carve a channel. Insight is real, but it works one layer above where the pattern lives.
questions.c: Insight works one layer above where the pattern lives

questions.q: What is the reinforcement loop, in Conversation 2.6?
o: Experience, impression, reactivation, action, a deeper groove, and a faster firing next time.
Memory, attention, judgement and action, which together make up one thoughtful choice.
Sleep, waking, work and rest, which together make up the rhythm of an ordinary day.
Thought, word and deed, which together make up what a person is seen to be by others.
questions.e: Left alone, the default is always reinforcement. But the same law runs in reverse: what you stop feeding silts up, and what you deliberately practise carves a new channel. This is slow, since you cannot carve a canyon in a day.
questions.c: Left alone, the default is reinforcement

questions.q: A woman wants to change an old pattern of fear. What does Conversation 2.6 say about how change works?
o: Stop feeding the old channel and deliberately practise a new one: slow, since no canyon is carved in a day.
Think about the fear until it is understood, since understanding is what clears the channel.
Wait for the fear to fade, since a groove that is left alone always grows shallower.
Fight the fear each time, since a strong enough effort will erase the groove at once.
questions.e: Left alone, the default is reinforcement. What you deliberately practise carves a new channel. This is the basis of all real change.
questions.c: Silt up the old channel; carve a new one slowly

questions.q: What does the hologram show in Conversation 2.6?
o: Each piece still holds the whole image, so each impression carries the quality of the whole field.
Each piece is a separate image, so that impressions do not affect one another at all.
Each piece is dimmer than the whole, so that small impressions can be ignored.
Each piece is lost when cut, so that memory fades as soon as it is divided up.
questions.e: Pribram’s holographic memory, the tree in the seed and the Gītā’s whole at every point converge here. So one deep wound can tint an entire personality, and one luminous impression of peace can begin to transform the whole field.
questions.c: The whole is in every part of the field

questions.q: “Clearing the field, chitta-śuddhi, means erasing memory so that nothing from the past remains.”
questions.e: Erasing memory would wipe out skill and love too. Chitta-śuddhi is re-landscaping: letting fear-cut channels silt up while carving clearer ones, through steady practice.
questions.c: Clearing the field is re-landscaping, not erasing

questions.q: In practice a man finds old patterns flooding up, and fears that he is failing. What does Conversation 2.6 say?
o: It is the stored material surfacing to be reworked: the patience is the path.
It is a sign of failure, so that he should stop the practice until it settles down.
It is a sign of illness, so that he should avoid practice for the rest of his life.
It is a sign that the practice is wrong, so that he should try a different one.
questions.e: When old patterns flood up in practice, that is not failure but the stored material surfacing to be reworked. The patience is the path.
questions.c: Old patterns surfacing is material to be reworked

questions.q: A woman blames herself for her persistent anxiety. How does Conversation 2.6 reframe it?
o: Retained patterns doing what patterns do, not a weakness: work at the level of the impression.
A weakness of character, which a stronger will could overcome if she tried a little harder.
A punishment for the past, which she must accept and carry as best she is able.
A mistake of thinking, which she can correct by simply deciding to think another way.
questions.e: Modern trauma-aware therapies, such as somatic work, EMDR, Internal Family Systems and trauma-informed mindfulness, converge with the ancient view: work at the level of the stored impression and not just the surface thought.
questions.c: Compassion, not blame: patterns doing what patterns do

questions.q: A teacher wants to tend her field this week. Which step fits Conversation 2.6?
o: Let one old channel go unfed, and carve a clearer one with a repeated word or breath.
Try to forget the whole of the past, so that no old channel is left to run in her mind.
Think over every old wound in turn, so that each is understood before she goes on.
Wait for a good mood to carve the new channel, since force has no part in change.
questions.e: Steady practice, a repeated word or breath, meditation, good company, service, and time with the true and beautiful, carves clearer channels while fear-cut ones silt up.
questions.c: Silt up one channel; carve one clearer channel
